Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:4: And there is an iniquity from which the soul cannot be cleared, and it remains impure and unaccepted, until death separates it from the body with which it sinned — just as there is a sickness from which the body will never be cleared all its days. This is the iniquity of desecrating the Name, as it is said (Isaiah 22:13), "and behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen and killing sheep, etc." — for they paid no heed to the words of the prophets and did not tremble because of them, but openly established, gathering companions together, various kinds of merrymaking. And of this it is said (Isaiah 22:14), "Surely this iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die." And it is said (II Chronicles 36:16), "But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised His words, and scoffed at His prophets, until the wrath of the Lord arose against His people, till there was no remedy."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:5: And even for this sickness, though it has no remedy in the manner of other iniquities, a remedy can be found for him if the Blessed Name helps him to sanctify His Torah before people, and to make known to people the might of the Name and the glorious splendor of His kingdom; and his iniquity departs through the very greatness of his excellent deeds, which are the opposite of the deed through which he acted foolishly and sinned — in the manner physicians say concerning bodily illness, that it is healed through its opposite, and its recovery comes about through its reversal. And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 16:6), "Through kindness and truth iniquity is atoned" — and we have already explained this in the First Gate of teshuvah. And the matter of "truth" mentioned there, its explanation is that the sinner prepare his heart to support the hands of truth, and to help those who seek faithfulness, and to remove falsehood and injustice — for making truth known and restoring it to its stronghold is the glory of God, in the sense of what is said (Jeremiah 22:16), "He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is this not to know Me?" And it is said concerning those who pursue falsehood (Jeremiah 9:5[6]), "through deceit they refuse to know Me." And our Sages of blessed memory said concerning Herod, who killed the sages, and asked counsel of Bava ben Buta whether he could find healing and a remedy for his affliction — and he said to him, You have extinguished the lamp of the world; go and occupy yourself with the light of the world, and strive for the building of the Holy Temple.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:6: Now let us explain the matter of the distinctions of atonement fully. Our Sages of blessed memory said (Yoma 86a): Rabbi Matya ben Charash asked Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah in Rome, Have you heard of the four distinctions of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael used to expound? He said to him: There are three, with teshuvah accompanying each and every one. If a man transgressed a positive commandment and did teshuvah, he does not move from there before he is forgiven immediately, as it is said (Jeremiah 3:22), "Return, backsliding children, I will heal your backslidings." If he transgressed a negative commandment and did teshuvah, teshuvah suspends the punishment and Yom Kippur atones, as it is said (Leviticus 16:30), "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall you be clean before the Lord." If he transgressed matters liable to excision or to death by the court and did teshuvah, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend the punishment, and sufferings scour it away, as it is said (Psalms 89:33), "then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with plagues." But one who has in his hand the iniquity of desecrating the Name — teshuvah has no power to suspend it, nor Yom Kippur to atone for it, nor suffering to scour it away, but all of these suspend it and death alone scours it away, as it is said (Isaiah 22:14), "Surely this iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die." And our Sages of blessed memory said: a burnt-offering atones for one who transgressed a positive commandment after teshuvah — for his iniquity is indeed already atoned through the teshuvah, but the burnt-offering adds to his atonement and adds further favor with the Blessed Name.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:7: They further said that a burnt-offering atones for what arises in a person's mind from stray thoughts of the heart and the contemplation of transgressions. And so it is written (Job 1:5), "And it was so, when the days of their feasting had run their course, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt-offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:8: Now, since we have no sacrifices, because of our sins and the sins of our fathers — if a man sinned in the stray thoughts of his heart, or transgressed a positive commandment, let him read the passage of the burnt-offering found at the beginning of the order of Vayikra and at the beginning of the order of Tzav et Aharon; for the reading of the passage of the offering will be for us in place of the actual offering of the sacrifice, whether read from a written text or recited by heart — as our Sages of blessed memory said, whoever occupies himself with the passage of the burnt-offering is as though he had offered a burnt-offering; with the passage of the sin-offering, as though he had offered a sin-offering; with the passage of the guilt-offering, as though he had offered a guilt-offering. And if a man transgressed a negative commandment and did teshuvah, let him worry over his iniquity and long and wait to reach Yom Kippur, so that he find favor with the Blessed Name; for His will is the life of the soul and the body, and the life of every creature, as it is said (Psalms 30:6), "life is in His favor." Therefore our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever holds a feast on the eve of Yom Kippur is as though he had been commanded to fast on the ninth and the tenth and had fasted on both — for he has shown his joy at the approach of the time of his atonement, and this shall be a testimony for him regarding his worry over his guilt and his grief over his iniquities.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:9: And the second reason [for this feast]: on other festivals we hold a feast for the joy of the commandment, for the reward for rejoicing over the commandments is very great and abundant, as it is said (I Chronicles 29:17), "and now I have seen with joy Your people who are present here, offering willingly to You," and it is said (Deuteronomy 28:47), "because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and gladness of heart." And because the fast falls on Yom Kippur itself, we are obligated to hold the feast for the joy of the commandment on the eve of Yom Kippur.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:10: And the third reason: so that we strengthen ourselves to increase prayer and supplication on Yom Kippur, and to take counsel with our souls concerning teshuvah and its foundations.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:11: And if a man transgressed matters liable to excision or death by the court and did teshuvah — since the iniquity is not accepted without suffering, for teshuvah suspends the punishment and suffering scours it away — let him prepare his heart to perform commandments that shield from suffering, such as the commandment of charity, for it saves even from death, as it is said (Proverbs 10:2), "but charity delivers from death." And one who has no money to give charity should speak well of the poor man and act as a mouthpiece to ask others to do good for him; and our Sages of blessed memory said, greater is one who causes others to give than one who gives himself. Likewise, let him occupy himself with the commandment of acts of kindness, to help his fellows with his counsel and his effort — as our Sages of blessed memory said, greater is the performance of acts of kindness than charity, for charity is with one's money, while acts of kindness may be either with one's body or with one's money; and charity is for the poor alone, while acts of kindness are for both the poor and the rich. Likewise, let him speak to the heart of the poor man and honor him and comfort him in his trouble, in the sense of what is said (Isaiah 58:10), "and pour out your soul to the hungry" — and our Sages, of blessed memory, said that one who consoles him with words is greater than one who gives him charity. Likewise, let him occupy himself with the commandment of visiting the sick, burying the dead, comforting mourners, and gladdening bride and groom, for all these are among the ways of kindness; and equal to all of them is the commandment of Torah study for the sake of Heaven. And all the counsels we have mentioned are included in what Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 16:6), "Through kindness and truth iniquity is atoned" — for the acquisition of Torah is called the acquisition of truth, as it is said (Proverbs 23:23), "Buy the truth, and sell it not," and it is said (Psalms 119:142), "and Your Torah is truth." And our Sages of blessed memory said, "It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it" (Proverbs 3:18). If a man transgressed matters liable to excision or death by the court — if he was accustomed to read one chapter a day, let him read two chapters; if he was accustomed to read one weekly portion, let him read two portions. And in two respects the Torah shields him from suffering: the first, as our Sages of blessed memory said, Torah study outweighs them all; and the second, that the labor he expends in Torah, his toil in it, and the sleep he drives from his eyes for it, take the place of suffering — as our Sages of blessed memory said, all bodies are born for toil; fortunate is he whose toil is in Torah. And they said, why is it called "tushiyah"? Because it wears down (mateshet) a person's strength.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:12: And likewise let him substitute for suffering fasts and afflictions, the shedding of tears, and the withholding of his soul from pleasures, as it is said (Psalms 109:24), "My knees are weak through fasting, and my flesh has grown lean from lack of fatness," and it is said (Joel 2:12), "Turn to Me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with lamentation." And let him sigh continually in bitterness of heart, as we mentioned in the First Gate of teshuvah; and let him substitute an abundance of bitterness for suffering, as it is said (Proverbs 18:14), "The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity, but a broken spirit who can bear?" Its meaning: when the body is sick, the soul bears its illness — in the sense of (Malachi 3:2), "but who can endure (mechalkel) the day of His coming" — meaning, it helps and sustains the body when it speaks to its heart and comforts it to accept and bear its suffering. But when the soul itself is sick and broken from grief and worry, who will comfort the soul, and who will bear and sustain it? Behold, worry and bitterness of heart are heavier than bodily illness, for the soul sustains the body in its illness, but when the soul itself is sick and broken from its own grief, the body cannot sustain it. And if you find the sinner in distress, and trouble befalls him, and he justifies the judgment upon himself and accepts the discipline with love, this shall be for him a shield from the many sufferings that would otherwise be fitting to come upon him — as it is said (Psalms 15... [likely intending a different psalm, kept as source numbering]), "For the wrath of man shall praise You; the residue of wrath shall You gird upon Yourself." Its meaning: when the distress of a man causes him to acknowledge and praise You — meaning, that the man acknowledges You at the time of his distress, in the sense of (Job 6:2), "Oh that my grief were but weighed," whose meaning is distress — "the residue of wrath" that was ready to come upon the man, You shall gird upon Yourself and restrain, and not bring them upon him — in the manner of (I Kings 20:11), "Let not him who girds on his armor boast as he who takes it off," [a figure] like one who unsheathes a sword and returns it to its scabbard. And it is said (Isaiah 12:1), "I will praise You, O Lord; for though You were angry with me, Your anger is turned away, and You comfort me." Its meaning: I praise You for Your discipline, and I have accepted it with love, and because of this — that I praise You for having been angry with me — Your anger is turned away and You comfort me. And likewise, concerning acknowledgment for good received, it is said (Psalms 52:11), "I will praise You forever, because You have done it; and I will wait on Your name, for it is good, before Your pious ones." Its meaning: I praise You for the good You have done for me, and because of this I hope for the continuation of Your goodness. And it is said (Psalms 116:13), "I will lift up the cup of salvations, and call upon the name of the Lord," (Psalms 116:3-4), "Trouble and sorrow I found, and I called upon the name of the Lord." And our Sages of blessed memory said, concerning what is written (Psalms 3:1), "A psalm of David, when he fled" — (Proverbs 21:15), "It is joy to the righteous to do justice." It is the trait of the righteous to pay their debt and sing to the Holy One, blessed be He, in a parable of a landowner who had a tenant farmer indebted to him; the tenant farmer worked the threshing floor and gathered it into a heap; the landowner took the heap, and the tenant farmer went home empty-handed, yet was joyful at going home empty-handed. They said to him, You have left your threshing floor with your hand upon your head, and yet you are joyful? He said to them, Even so, the debt-note is wiped clean — I have paid my debt.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:13: And a man is obligated to consider and know that the trouble that has found him and the sufferings that come upon him are not in proportion to the greatness of his iniquity and the abundance of his sins; rather, the Blessed Name disciplines him in the manner a father disciplines his son, out of the Lord's compassion upon him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:5), "And you shall know in your heart, that just as a man chastens his son, the Lord your God chastens you." And our Sages of blessed memory said [as though quoted from God]: Your own heart knows the deeds you have done and the sufferings I have brought upon you, that I have not disciplined you in proportion to your deeds. And it is said (Job 11:6), "know therefore that God exacts of you less than your iniquity deserves," and it is said (Ezra 9:13), "seeing that You our God have punished us less than our iniquities deserve." And when discipline comes upon the enemies of the Blessed Lord, they are wiped out for a single iniquity, for retribution comes upon them all at once, as it is said (Psalms 34:22), "Evil shall slay the wicked," and the rest of their iniquities remain upon their own souls, as it is said (Ezekiel 32:27), "and their iniquities shall be upon their bones." But when discipline comes upon the righteous, it comes little by little, until their iniquities are exhausted, as it is said (Amos 3:2), "You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities." And our Sages of blessed memory explained this with a parable: like one who lent to two men, one his friend and one his enemy — from his friend he collects little by little, but from his enemy he collects all at once. And it is said (Proverbs 24:16), "For a righteous man falls seven times, and rises up again, but the wicked stumble into calamity." Its meaning: they stumble into one calamity and are finished. And it is said (Jeremiah 10:24), "O Lord, correct me, but with judgment; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing." Its meaning of "but with judgment": according to the measure of Your mercy and the rule of Your kindnesses, in the sense of (Numbers 29:18), "according to their number, after the ordinance (kamishpat)" meaning according to the statute, (Psalms 112:5), "he will guide his affairs with discretion (bemishpat)" meaning by proper measure. And they gave a further parable concerning this matter, saying: one who does not know how to strike strikes his son on his eyes and his face, but one who knows how to strike, strikes his son in a manner that does not harm him. And so it is written (Psalms 118:18), "The Lord has chastened me severely, but He has not given me over to death," and it is said (Job 2:6), "only spare his life." And upon the wicked come only vengeful sufferings, but the sufferings of testing come only upon the righteous, who accept them with love and add correction to their deeds, and the sufferings are for their good and their benefit and the greatness of their reward, as it is said (Psalms 11:5), "the Lord tests the righteous." And our Sages of blessed memory gave a parable for this and said: when the owner of flax knows that the flax is strong, he beats it much, to make it soft and good.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:14: Now let us return to the matter of our discussion concerning the order of atonements, and say: when a man inadvertently transgresses matters liable to excision or death by the court, he is obligated to confess and to seek supplication for forgiveness, and to sigh in bitterness of heart, and to worry and to fear — for these are among the foundations of atonement. And let him occupy himself continually with the passage of the sin-offering, and it shall be reckoned to him as though he had offered a sin-offering — meaning, it will greatly benefit him and he will be atoned in the manner resembling the atonement of the sin-offering.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:15: And know that even the one who transgresses inadvertently shall surely be punished, as we have already stated earlier — how much more so the one who acted with presumption, meaning one who erred in a matter that people are accustomed to be careful about; and he ought to worry and fear because of his sin. And our Sages of blessed memory said, in explaining what is written (Psalms 48:3), "Beautiful in situation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King" — that when a man transgressed a transgression inadvertently, his heart would worry over it, and he would tremble and fear because of his sin, until he went up to Jerusalem and offered the sin-offering sacrifice, and then he would be joyful. Of this it is said, "Beautiful in situation, the joy of the whole earth." And what it says, "on the sides of the north," speaks of the altar, for "the sides of the north" was the joy of the whole earth, since the sin-offering was slaughtered on the north side of the altar. And our Sages of blessed memory said: when a man commits a transgression and continually turns it over in his heart, thinking about his sin which he committed, and trembles and fears because of it, the Holy One, blessed be He, forgives him. But when he puts a transgression out of his mind, and it is small and light in his eyes, his case is like one who was bitten by a scorpion and scorns the bite, and presses his foot on the ground to disperse the venom, while onlookers say to him, Do you not know that it will rise from the sole of your foot to your crown?
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:16: Now let us speak of one who has in his hand the iniquity of desecrating the Name, whose iniquity is not atoned through suffering. And we have already stated that he has a remedy if he continually sanctifies the Blessed Name; further, he can find atonement through continually meditating on the Torah and toiling in it, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Jerusalem Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 2:5): could the iniquity of the house of Eli be atoned through sacrifice and meal-offering? Through sacrifice and meal-offering it cannot be atoned, but it can be atoned through words of Torah. And even though the iniquity of the house of Eli was regarding the desecration of the commandment concerning sacred things, as it is said (I Samuel 3:13), "for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons brought a curse upon themselves" — behold, the Torah is a remedy for every most grievous wound; therefore it is written (Proverbs 15:4), "A healing tongue is a tree of life."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:17: And concerning what they said, of blessed memory, that for matters liable to excision or death by the court, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend the punishment and suffering scours it away — there is a question: is it not written (Leviticus 16:30), "from all your sins shall you be clean before the Lord"? The answer to this is that what is said, "before the Lord shall you be clean," is a positive commandment concerning teshuvah — that we search and examine our ways and return to the Lord on Yom Kippur; and even though we are obligated in this at all times, the obligation is increased on Yom Kippur, and the purity that is in our own hands is teshuvah and the correction of our deeds. But what is written there, "for on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you," is said concerning the purity that the Blessed Name purifies us from iniquity and grants us complete atonement on Yom Kippur without suffering — this is said concerning negative commandments; but concerning matters liable to excision or death by the court, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend the punishment and suffering scours it away.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:18: And our Sages of blessed memory said: "from all your sins shall you be clean before the Lord" — transgressions between man and the Omnipresent are atoned by Yom Kippur; transgressions between a man and his fellow are not atoned by Yom Kippur until he has appeased his fellow. Therefore whoever robbed his fellow should restore the stolen object, and only afterward confess; and if he confessed first, the confession does not count for him — as our Sages of blessed memory said concerning the robber who also swore falsely, that he is obligated to pay the principal plus a fifth and to bring a guilt-offering: whoever brings his restitution before he brings his guilt-offering has fulfilled his obligation, but whoever brings his guilt-offering before he brings his restitution has not fulfilled his obligation — as it is said, concerning the robbery of a convert who has no heirs, where the payment is given to the priest (Numbers 5:8), "the guilt-offering being restored to the Lord, even to the priest, besides the ram of atonement, whereby atonement shall be made for him." Its meaning: the "guilt-offering" mentioned in this verse refers to the restitution payment, in the sense of (Numbers 5:7), "and he shall give it to him against whom he has trespassed (asham)" — and he brings the restitution payment, besides the ram of atonement whereby atonement is made for him afterward.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:19: And our Sages of blessed memory said: if a man provoked his fellow with words, he must appease him — and how much more so if he spoke evil speech about him, for this is among the grave transgressions. And if his fellow does not forgive him, he is obligated to come before him with a group of three men; and if he still does not forgive him, he should come before him a second time with another group; and he should do so a third time. And Elihu said (Job 33:27-28), "He looks upon men, and says, I have sinned, and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me." Its meaning: "I perverted the upright man," in the sense of (Job 1:1), "whole-hearted and upright (tam v'yashar)" — meaning, I did not see merit in the upright man, but rather made him crooked and perverse, and he was not treated as fair and upright by me, and "it was not repaid to me" — in the sense of "if her face is level (hishvah)" (Isaiah 28:25), "to the plain (emek shaveh)" (Genesis 14:17) — the matter of leveling and equating. And since he demeaned the upright before other people, he must submit before them and confess publicly; therefore it says, "He looks upon men" [confessing publicly]. And Elihu spoke of this particular sin specifically because it is among the grave transgressions that destroy the soul. And our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever demeans a Torah scholar has no remedy for his wound, because he has desecrated the Torah, as it is said (II Chronicles 36:16), "But they mocked the messengers of God, etc., till there was no remedy."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:20: And what our Sages of blessed memory said, that one who has in his hand the desecration of the Name — teshuvah, Yom Kippur, and suffering suspend the punishment, and death scours it away — this is because death scours away every sin for which teshuvah is of avail. And if such a man was executed and confessed before his death, from the time the terrors of death fell upon him, he has atonement, and the executioner is reckoned as one who shed innocent and pious blood, as it is said (Psalms 79:2), "the flesh of Your pious ones to the beasts of the earth." And our Sages of blessed memory said that this is said even of the wicked among them, as it is said of them (Jeremiah 5:8), "They were as fed horses in the morning" — for they are reckoned as pious ones, since the judgment has been executed upon them, as it is written, "and your brother be dishonored before your eyes" — once he has been punished, he is like your brother.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:21: And our Sages of blessed memory said: transgressions for which a man confessed on this Yom Kippur — he confesses them again on another Yom Kippur, as it is said (Psalms 51:5), "and my sin is ever before me." Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: he does not confess them again on another Yom Kippur. And in the Midrashim they warned strongly that one should not go back and confess them again on another Yom Kippur, and they warned of this for two reasons. The first: because he thereby shows himself to be of little trust, as though he does not trust in the greatness of the Blessed Name's forgiveness, that He forgives iniquity and passes over transgression; and of this they mentioned (Psalms 31:19), "Let lying lips be dumb, etc." And the second: because if he mentions nothing but his previous iniquities, it will seem that his worry is only over the earlier ones, and that he has not sinned since then; and if so, it will seem that he does not search and examine his ways — and this is an evil sickness. For those who watch over their souls continually see in themselves matters of iniquity, whether in their character traits, or in that they fall short in attaining the levels of fear, or in that they fall short in service and in occupation with Torah — for the punishments for these are great, and moreover, transgressions of the tongue are common. And our Sages of blessed memory said: from three things a man is not saved every day — the thought of transgression, the dust of evil speech, and that they do not direct their hearts in their prayer many times. And the third reason: he will seem to boast, by confessing only the earlier sins, that he has not sinned since then. And they said in the Midrashim: because you have nothing new, you confess the old ones. And what is written, "and my sin is ever before me," they explained in the Midrash that it should be before his eyes and remembered in his heart, but he should not mention it with his mouth. They further explained it in the Jerusalem Talmud: they should not seem in your own eyes as though you had not done them, but as though you had done them and they had been forgiven — and we have already mentioned this in the Gates of the Foundations of Teshuvah. Indeed, he should seek mercy all the days of his life for the forgiveness of his earlier and later iniquities, and be fearful and afraid lest he has not fully discharged the obligation of the foundations of teshuvah. And the second point: transgressions that carry excision are scoured away by suffering, as we have mentioned; and David the king, peace upon him, also said (Psalms 25:7), "Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions" — yet he does not mention the earlier ones in particular, since he had already turned back from them and confessed them on Yom Kippur, having already fulfilled the commandment of confession regarding them, and he may trust that his confession has already been accepted insofar as confession is fitting to atone. Nevertheless, all his days he should pray for the forgiveness of his iniquities, as we have mentioned; but it is not an obligation of prayer to specify one's sins — that is an obligation of confession alone. And for a further reason one must pray concerning the iniquities of earlier days: for perhaps he has iniquities and sins he did not consider, did not remember, and did not confess — in the sense of what is said (Psalms 19:13), "Clear me from hidden faults."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:22: And the order of confession is: "We have sinned (chatanu), we have committed iniquity (avinu), we have transgressed (pashanu)." "Chet" (sin) includes both the inadvertent transgression and the presumptuous one; and the matter of presumption, in the language of the Sages of Israel, is when a man is not careful in a matter that people are accustomed to be careful about, as we have stated earlier. "Avonot" (iniquities) are deliberate transgressions, and "pesha'im" (transgressions/rebellions) are acts of rebellion, in the sense of (II Kings 3:7), "the king of Moab has rebelled (pasha) against me." And the Blessed Name forgives, in the greatness of His kindness, even those who rebel against Him, if they return to Him with all their heart; and it is said (Daniel 9:9), "To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses, though we have rebelled against Him," and it is said (Psalms 25:11), "For Your name's sake, O Lord, pardon my iniquity, for it is great," and it is said (Psalms 65:4), "Matters of iniquities have overwhelmed me; as for our transgressions, You shall atone for them."
